facts.claim: "Let's Talk About Your Hair" is track 6 on Have Mercy's debut LP The Earth Pushed Back, released May 21, 2013, and runs 3:55.
The Earth Pushed Back first came out on Topshelf Records (cat. TSR081). Rude Records lists the 2022 Spotify reissue.
The song was written by Brian Swindle and produced by J. Robbins. Deezer lists the writing credit as Swindle, Andrew Johnson, Nick Woolford and Aaron Alt.
Deezer's composer credit for the track is Brian Swindle, Andrew Johnson, Nick Woolford and Aaron Alt.

Album credits list Brian Swindle, Aaron Alt, Nick Woolford and Andrew Johnson as performers. J. Robbins is credited as producer, recording engineer and mixer, Justin Fogleman as engineer, and Dan Coutant as mastering engineer.
The album was recorded at The Magpie Cage in the band's hometown of Baltimore, with J. Robbins producing.

Swindle said the LP was recorded in five days, after the debut EP My Oldest Friend took four. In another interview he said the album was rushed and the band had to write two or three songs in the studio.
Swindle said The Earth Pushed Back is about one relationship he had, though it also touches on multiple other subjects.
Before the album's release, Swindle called The Earth Pushed Back his favorite record he'd performed on, with a more raw sound and more powerful songs. He also praised working with J. Robbins.
Have Mercy is a Baltimore band. Swindle said the group got a record deal soon after releasing its first EP, and the follow-up A Place of Our Own (2014) was produced by Paul Leavitt.

research.lineage: The song sits in the 2010s emo revival, where Rate Your Music places the album, and a 2013 profile compared the record's audience to fans of Brand New, Tigers Jaw and Taking Back Sunday.

draft:
The most devastating move in **Let's Talk About Your Hair** is how small the subject is. Two people have reached the point where the truth is out and nobody will say it, and so the conversation turns to the most harmless thing in the room: "Let's talk about your hair and how it's grown." It's a gesture of surrender, and it's also a way of noticing time. Hair grows while you aren't paying attention. So did the distance.

Have Mercy's Brian Swindle wrote the song (Deezer splits the credit across the whole band: Swindle, Andrew Johnson, Nick Woolford, Aaron Alt), and he said the album it anchors, *The Earth Pushed Back*, is about one relationship. You can hear the tangle in the refrain's stutter: "I know that you know that I know that you don't really care." It's a hall of mirrors built out of plain words. Each "know" piles on another layer of awareness, and none of it changes anything. The narrator wants credit for seeing clearly while admitting, two lines earlier, "I can't see clearly." Both are true, and the song doesn't settle it.

Then comes the line that gives the whole thing away: "Tell me about the man in your dreams / And was it me?" Under all the resignation sits a hope that hasn't died. The verse's dream, with "a god, a devil, and me," casts the other person as the one who lost their wings, a fall the narrator half-blames and half-mourns. When the verse returns, "we went to bed that night" has become "I went to bed." That one pronoun is the breakup. Near the end even "and how it's grown" drops away, as if the small talk itself is wearing out.

The band plays it like a shout. Drums drive with a hard snare and crashing cymbals, bass sits on the roots, one distorted guitar chugs palm-muted while another holds a higher, sustained line above it. The vocal is raw and slightly strained, with no harmonies to soften it. J. Robbins produced, recorded and mixed the record at The Magpie Cage in the band's hometown of Baltimore, and the sound is thick, compressed and live in the room, unpolished on purpose. Swindle said the album was cut in five days and felt rushed, but he also called it his favorite record, more raw and more powerful than what came before.

It belongs to the 2010s emo revival, the scene a 2013 profile tied to fans of Brand New, Tigers Jaw and Taking Back Sunday, and it carries that tradition's gift for turning a single overheard sentence into a wound.

It sticks because you know the move: when you can't bear to ask the real question, you ask about something small, and then you ask the real one anyway.

factCheck.claim: Refrain quote: "I know that you know that I know that you don't really care."
factCheck.note: The wording matches the lyrics, but the draft quoted far more than three lines overall. Paraphrased the refrain to stay within the quote limit.

factCheck.claim: The narrator admits "I can't see clearly" two lines earlier than the refrain.
factCheck.note: The line comes immediately before the refrain (across a stanza break), not two lines earlier. Paraphrased and fixed the placement.

factCheck.claim: Near the end the line "and how it's grown" drops away.
